1  Introduction

Science advances through successive cycles of inquiry, with the outcomes of each cycle forming the foundation for the next. At the frontier, researchers probe the implications and limits of existing knowledge, developing abstractions that reveal new questions and give them a precise form. These questions frame an inquiry in which conjectures guide proof and experiment and are revised in light of the resulting insights and counterexamples. Supported advances and exposed limits emerging from this inquiry are consolidated into the body of knowledge, reshaping the frontier and the methods available to explore it. This recursive view of scientific progress has clear precedents in accounts of conjecture and refutation, paradigm change, and evolving research programmes (Popper, 1963; Kuhn, 1962; Lakatos, 1978).

Historically, human researchers have been the main drivers of this continual renewal. In the AI era, machines are increasingly contributing to scientific discovery, from protein structure prediction and materials discovery to new algorithms and mathematical constructions (Jumper et al., 2021; Merchant et al., 2023; Fawzi et al., 2022; Romera-Paredes et al., 2024). Agentic systems extend this involvement to the organization of research, coordinating problem formulation, investigation, and validation, with increasing support for autonomous topic selection and knowledge reuse (Lu et al., 2024; Yamada et al., 2025; Gottweis et al., 2025; Mitchener et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Tan and Syrgkanis, 2026; Kim et al., 2026). Yet a broader challenge remains: enabling systems to understand a field’s evolving frontier and use that understanding to direct sustained research. This requires assessing what is known, where existing results hold, and which unresolved questions matter for further progress, then selecting and pursuing investigations on that basis. As research yields new findings and exposes limitations, the system must revise its understanding of the frontier and its research agenda, reusing accumulated knowledge and research experience to pursue further advances. The aim is thus to extend autonomy from completing individual investigations to sustaining research from frontier to frontier.

We introduce Colombo, a self-organizing AI researcher that pursues this objective in oracle-based optimization.11 1 This paper was previously deposited on Zenodo:https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23438699. In this domain, algorithms access problem instances through prescribed information interfaces, and complexity analysis asks how efficiently a task can be solved over a declared model class and which resource requirements are unavoidable for every admissible algorithm (Nemirovski and Yudin, 1983; Nesterov, 2004). This information-based perspective is foundational to the analysis of iterative methods used in large-scale model training, online prediction, and sequential decision and control (Bottou et al., 2018; Hazan, 2016; Recht, 2019; Nemirovski and Yudin, 1983; Nesterov, 2004). Its research frontier is explicit: algorithm design establishes achievable guarantees, hardness constructions establish unavoidable limits, and any mismatch between them identifies a concrete research frontier. Colombo organizes the continual investigation of this frontier through two complementary mechanisms: Self-Organization structures and directs inquiry, while Adversarial Co-Ascent generates new knowledge through targeted scientific challenge. Figure 1 illustrates this frontier-to-frontier renewal.

Self-Organization operates frontier-to-frontier research through a field–programme–problem hierarchy. At the field level, the Sensorium maps complexity settings and the gaps between achievable guarantees and unavoidable costs. At the programme level, the Brain conjectures optimal rates, develops technical routes, and decomposes the required constructions and proofs into precise subproblems. At the problem level, Cells adaptively investigate these subproblems. Their evidence guides the Brain’s monitoring and replanning, focusing successive rounds on the remaining gap. Validated findings refine the Atlas, while accumulated mechanisms inform new settings and programmes, linking progress within individual settings to the continual renewal of the research frontier.

Adversarial Co-Ascent supplies the knowledge-generating dynamic of Colombo. In oracle-based optimization, algorithms probe candidate hard families for exploitable structure, while hard instances challenge how candidate methods acquire and use information. By isolating the properties behind these successes and failures, the system develops conjectures about what makes algorithms effective and problems difficult. These conjectures guide new algorithms and sharper hardness constructions; proving or refuting them clarifies the conditions under which the proposed mechanisms hold and reveals what remains to be understood. Established insights become reusable knowledge that can improve complexity guarantees and distinguish new problem classes. Accumulated in the Long-Term Memory, this knowledge shapes subsequent investigations, turning reciprocal challenge into the continued advancement and renewal of the research frontier.

In its current deployment, Colombo has obtained optimal or near-optimal rates for more than fifty settings in the Complexity Atlas. This report presents the architecture and research mechanisms underlying these investigations, summarizes their principal research outcomes in Section 3, and examines how the framework could be adapted to applied optimization. In model training, Adversarial Co-Ascent could extend to capability–challenge co-evolution: stronger training methods may render existing benchmarks less informative, while targeted diagnostic challenges can expose failure modes that motivate new algorithms and training procedures. Across successive cycles, the accumulated evidence could motivate new training regimes and parameterizations, reveal scaling relations, and guide subsequent investigations. By organizing frontier-to-frontier research in oracle-based optimization, Colombo provides initial evidence for the feasibility of Autopoietic Science, introduced in Section 4 as the vision of a scientific process whose validated advances continually renew both its understanding and the conditions through which further discovery becomes possible.

2  System Architecture: From Frontier to Frontier

Colombo is designed to autonomously advance and renew the research frontier of oracle-based optimization. It represents this frontier at two coupled levels. At the field level, the Sensorium maintains a Complexity Atlas of mathematically specified complexity settings and the relations among them; the Atlas expands as the system identifies new settings or establishes new connections among existing ones. At the setting level, the Sensorium prepares a Setting Profile containing the setting’s mathematical specification and its Complexity Bracket—the best-supported upper and lower bounds across the relevant parameter regimes. The Profile is passed to the Brain, which turns the unresolved gap in that bracket into concrete research subproblems for Research Cells and governs their investigation through repeated rounds of planning, monitoring, replanning, and integration. Candidate resolutions then undergo independent review and formal certification. Validated theorems, algorithms, hard families, proof techniques, and negative evidence are retained in Scientific Memory, while certified setting and bound updates are written back to the Atlas. A completed programme may therefore deepen the frontier by tightening or closing the bracket of an existing setting, broaden it by extending the Atlas, or do both. For the research reported in this paper, Colombo was instantiated with GPT-5.6 Sol as its underlying language model.

The remainder of this section presents the Sensorium for frontier sensing and setting characterization (Subsection 2.1), the Brain for research planning and adaptive governance (Subsection 2.2), Cells for subproblem investigation (Subsection 2.3), Formal Certification for Lean-based proof verification and claim alignment (Subsection 2.4), the Paper Composer for turning certified research records into scientific papers (Subsection 2.5), and the Memory for preserving active research state and reusable knowledge across research cycles (Subsection 2.6). Figure 2 summarizes this frontier-to-frontier architecture and the flow of information between its major components.

2.1  Sensorium

The Sensorium is the frontier-perception layer of Colombo. It performs two coupled functions: it maintains a structured view of which complexity settings have been identified in oracle-based optimization, how they are related, and how far each has been resolved; and it prepares an audited Setting Profile for a selected setting, recording its mathematical specification, current upper and lower bounds, supporting evidence, and the modeling choices that remain open to the Brain.

2.1.1  The Complexity Atlas

The Complexity Atlas is a relational map of complexity settings in oracle-based optimization. Each node represents a complexity setting: a mathematically specified model in which the task, admissible instance or function class, domain geometry, regularity assumptions, oracle or feedback interface, resource measure, and success criterion jointly define a well-posed optimal-complexity question. A setting is therefore already concrete enough to support precise theorem statements and meaningful comparisons of upper and lower bounds. What remains open to the Brain are programme-level choices rather than the core mathematical identity of the setting—for example, which parameter regime to prioritize, whether to pursue deterministic or randomized guarantees first, which side of the gap to attack, and what intermediate notion of near-optimality to accept. Algorithms are adaptive by default unless the research scope states otherwise, and every resulting bound is tagged with the exact algorithmic model and parameter regime under which it holds.

A setting may exhibit different optimal rates across parameter regimes—for example, low- and high-accuracy regimes, dimension-limited and dimension-saturated regimes, or different condition-number ranges. The Atlas records this piecewise structure internally and assigns a bound status to each regime. A regime is optimal when its best-supported upper and lower bounds match under the declared asymptotic convention; near-optimal when the remaining discrepancy is only logarithmic or polylogarithmic; open when a substantive gap remains; upper-only or lower-only when one side is missing; and uncharacterized when no reliable bounds picture has yet been established. For field-level display, each setting receives a conservative aggregate status determined by its least-resolved relevant regime: it is marked optimal only when all such regimes are optimal, and near-optimal only when every regime is at least near-optimal. Any open, one-sided, or uncharacterized regime keeps the setting correspondingly unresolved on the Atlas.

The Atlas is initially constructed through a systematic survey of established oracle-based optimization settings and their best-known complexity bounds, and is subsequently revised through three complementary modes of discovery. Literature-grounded discovery identifies stated open problems and detects unresolved gaps by aligning upper- and lower-bound results reported across separate sources. Structural exploration varies the defining elements of established settings—most notably the oracle model and the geometry or regularity of the problem class—to identify adjacent complexity questions that merit separate treatment. Memory-driven discovery mines prior investigations for recurring algorithms, hardness mechanisms, proof ideas, and failure patterns that point to settings not yet represented. Relations between nodes record how settings differ and whether theoretical insights can transfer across those differences. The Complexity Atlas thereby makes the research frontier explicit along two coupled dimensions: the breadth of the setting space that has been discovered and characterized, and the extent to which the upper–lower gap within each represented setting has been resolved.

2.1.2  The Setting Profile

A Setting Profile is the Sensorium’s audited account of a selected setting. Let ss label the setting and 𝖲s\mathsf{S}_{s} denote its mathematical specification. The Profile is 𝒫s=(𝖲s,ℬs,ℰs)\mathcal{P}_{s}=(\mathsf{S}_{s},\mathcal{B}_{s},\mathcal{E}_{s}), where ℬs\mathcal{B}_{s} is the Complexity Bracket and ℰs\mathcal{E}_{s} records its supporting evidence. Together, these components specify what is being studied, which guarantees are currently supported, and where further progress is needed.

Setting specification.

The setting specification 𝖲s\mathsf{S}_{s} fixes the task, the models under consideration, and the conditions under which an algorithm may solve it:

𝖲s=(𝖳s,ℐs​(θ),𝒵s,ℓs,𝒪s,𝒜s,cs).\mathsf{S}_{s}=\bigl(\mathsf{T}_{s},\mathcal{I}_{s}(\theta),\mathcal{Z}_{s},\ell_{s};\ \mathcal{O}_{s},\mathcal{A}_{s},c_{s}\bigr). (1)

The task formulation 𝖳s\mathsf{T}_{s} specifies the mathematical structure to be solved. The admissible model class ℐs​(θ)\mathcal{I}_{s}(\theta) consists of the objectives, operators, or structured models satisfying the declared geometric, regularity, and structural assumptions. The parameters θ\theta quantify these restrictions and the problem scale, such as dimension, smoothness and strong-convexity constants, or domain size. A member I∈ℐs​(θ)I\in\mathcal{I}_{s}(\theta) fixes one concrete model satisfying these assumptions. In stochastic settings, it also specifies the relevant data or observation laws. For each such model, the output space 𝒵s\mathcal{Z}_{s} specifies the form and ambient domain of the result an algorithm must produce. The performance measure ℓs​(I,z)\ell_{s}(I,z) quantifies how accurately an output zz fulfills the declared solution requirement. The oracle model 𝒪s\mathcal{O}_{s} determines the permitted access to each model, including public inputs and query feedback. The admissible algorithm class 𝒜s\mathcal{A}_{s} comprises the procedures allowed under this information model and the declared computational restrictions, including restrictions on adaptivity, randomization, or communication. The resource convention csc_{s} specifies the resource counted in the complexity analysis, such as oracle calls, samples, or communication rounds.

Performance guarantees and complexity.

For an accuracy-based target, fix an error tolerance ε>0\varepsilon>0 and an allowed failure probability δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), and write η=(ε,δ,θ)\eta=(\varepsilon,\delta,\theta). Each A∈𝒜sA\in\mathcal{A}_{s} specifies its query, stopping, and output rules, including any prescribed execution budget. Let ZA,IZ^{A,I} denote its returned outcome and cs​(A,I)c_{s}(A,I) its scalar resource cost, evaluated using the Profile’s expected-cost or almost-sure cost convention. To compare algorithms under the same accuracy requirement, define

Ns​(A,I,η):={cs​(A,I),ℙA,I​(ℓs​(I,ZA,I)>ε)≤δ,+∞,otherwise.N_{s}(A,I;\eta):=\begin{cases}c_{s}(A,I),&\mathbb{P}_{A,I}\!\left(\ell_{s}(I,Z^{A,I})>\varepsilon\right)\leq\delta,\\[2.0pt] +\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

The first branch records the cost of attaining error at most ε\varepsilon with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta; the probability includes algorithmic and observational randomness. The optimal complexity is

Ns⋆​(ε,δ,θ):=infA∈𝒜ssupI∈ℐs​(θ)Ns​(A,I,η).N_{s}^{\star}(\varepsilon,\delta;\theta):=\inf_{A\in\mathcal{A}_{s}}\sup_{I\in\mathcal{I}_{s}(\theta)}N_{s}(A,I;\eta).

The same algorithm must meet the requirement on every admissible model; if no finite uniform cost is achievable, Ns⋆=+∞N_{s}^{\star}=+\infty. For a resource budget n≥0n\geq 0, 𝒜s​(n)\mathcal{A}_{s}(n) contains the procedures satisfying supI∈ℐs​(θ)cs​(A,I)≤n\sup_{I\in\mathcal{I}_{s}(\theta)}c_{s}(A,I)\leq n. The performance measure need not itself be observable through the oracle.

Complexity Bracket.

Upper and lower bounds characterize the achievable and unavoidable resource requirements under the mathematical specification. Fix (ε,δ,θ)(\varepsilon,\delta,\theta), and suppress these arguments in LsL_{s} and UsU_{s} when stating the bound conditions.

An upper bound follows from an admissible algorithm that meets the accuracy requirement within budget UsU_{s} uniformly over the model class:

∃A∈𝒜s(Us),∀I∈ℐs(θ):ℙA,I(ℓs(I,ZA,I)>ε)≤δ⟹Ns⋆(ε,δ;θ)≤Us.\displaystyle\exists A\in\mathcal{A}_{s}(U_{s}),\ \forall I\in\mathcal{I}_{s}(\theta):\ \mathbb{P}_{A,I}\!\left(\ell_{s}(I,Z^{A,I})>\varepsilon\right)\leq\delta\ \Longrightarrow\ N_{s}^{\star}(\varepsilon,\delta;\theta)\leq U_{s}.

A lower bound establishes that every smaller budget is insufficient: each admissible algorithm exceeds the allowed failure probability on at least one model in the class:

∀n∈[0,Ls),∀A∈𝒜s(n),∃I∈ℐs(θ):ℙA,I(ℓs(I,ZA,I)>ε)>δ⟹Ns⋆(ε,δ;θ)≥Ls.\displaystyle\forall n\in[0,L_{s}),\ \forall A\in\mathcal{A}_{s}(n),\ \exists I\in\mathcal{I}_{s}(\theta):\ \mathbb{P}_{A,I}\!\left(\ell_{s}(I,Z^{A,I})>\varepsilon\right)>\delta\ \Longrightarrow\ N_{s}^{\star}(\varepsilon,\delta;\theta)\geq L_{s}.

The Complexity Bracket ℬs\mathcal{B}_{s} records the strongest currently supported applicable bounds of these two kinds:

Ls​(ε,δ,θ)≤Ns⋆​(ε,δ,θ)≤Us​(ε,δ,θ).L_{s}(\varepsilon,\delta;\theta)\leq N_{s}^{\star}(\varepsilon,\delta;\theta)\leq U_{s}(\varepsilon,\delta;\theta).

Both boundaries concern the same task, model class, oracle model, admissible algorithm class, accuracy requirement, and resource convention. Their expressions and domains of validity may vary across parameter regimes. Accordingly, ℬs\mathcal{B}_{s} is an interval-valued map on the parameter domain. For a partition into regions 𝒟s,1,…,𝒟s,Js\mathcal{D}_{s,1},\ldots,\mathcal{D}_{s,J_{s}}, it is recorded as

ℬs​(ε,δ,θ)={[Ls,1​(ε,δ,θ),Us,1​(ε,δ,θ)],(ε,δ,θ)∈𝒟s,1,[Ls,Js​(ε,δ,θ),Us,Js​(ε,δ,θ)],(ε,δ,θ)∈𝒟s,Js.\mathcal{B}_{s}(\varepsilon,\delta;\theta)=\begin{cases}[L_{s,1}(\varepsilon,\delta;\theta),U_{s,1}(\varepsilon,\delta;\theta)],&(\varepsilon,\delta,\theta)\in\mathcal{D}_{s,1},\\[4.0pt] \vdots&\vdots\\[4.0pt] [L_{s,J_{s}}(\varepsilon,\delta;\theta),U_{s,J_{s}}(\varepsilon,\delta;\theta)],&(\varepsilon,\delta,\theta)\in\mathcal{D}_{s,J_{s}}.\end{cases}

The partition records both changes in the dominant bounds and restrictions on their validity. Each region therefore has its own supported bounds and unresolved gap: matching bounds in one region may coexist with an open gap in another. If a side has no supported nontrivial bound, the Profile marks it as unknown and uses 00 as the trivial lower endpoint or +∞+\infty as the trivial upper endpoint.

The evidence record ℰs\mathcal{E}_{s} links each bound to its source theorem or proof, assumptions, parameter domain, and review or certification status. The Sensorium aligns notation, confidence requirements, resource conventions, and asymptotic comparisons, and checks any transfer from a neighboring setting against the declared mathematical specification. Each comparison therefore concerns compatible bounds on the same complexity quantity over a common domain of validity.

The resulting Profile identifies the unresolved parameter regimes and supplies the mathematical evidence from which the Brain can select target rates and research routes.

2.1.3  Research Entry Modes

The Sensorium supports two entry modes. In autonomous mode, it searches the unresolved regions of the Complexity Atlas and ranks candidate Setting Profiles by scientific importance and estimated tractability. In scope-guided mode, a user provides a research scope. The Sensorium combines that scope with the current Atlas, literature search, neighboring-setting exploration, and Scientific Memory to identify and characterize the most consequential candidate settings. Newly identified settings are added to the Atlas with provisional status. In either mode, a human approval gate selects the Setting Profile to be passed to the Brain.

2.2  Brain

At the programme level, the Brain transforms a selected Setting Profile into an adaptive research programme for resolving the gap represented by its Complexity Bracket. It determines the research target, decomposes the unresolved gap into coordinated subproblems, directs their investigation, and revises the programme as evidence accumulates. The Brain thus carries a setting from an audited frontier description to a review-ready natural-language result, rather than merely decomposing a fixed problem once.

Research proceeds on two nested timescales. A research round is the unit of programme-level planning and revision: using reasoning, search, experiments, and memory, the Brain deploys one versioned batch of research subproblems, monitors its execution, and subsequently integrates the evidence produced by the batch as a whole. Within a research round, each Cell performs a sequence of shorter Cell iterations. Every Cell iteration ends with a local audit, an updated draft and working memory, and a checkpoint report to the Brain. Cells reach their checkpoints independently. Upon receiving each report, the Brain updates the Live Complexity Bracket and its short-term programme memory. The revised shared state informs both the reporting Cell’s continuation and the subsequent iterations of other Cells. At that checkpoint, the Brain may allow the Cell to continue, pause it, or provide limited strategic guidance. Once all Cells in the batch have reached a stopping point, the Brain integrates their outputs and determines whether the declared optimality target has been reached. A successful round proceeds to synthesis, independent review, and formal certification; an unresolved Complexity Bracket triggers targeted replanning and a new research round.

Combining reasoning, search, experiments, and memory, the Brain prioritizes unresolved parameter regimes, selects the advances to pursue, and develops routes toward them. Upper-bound routes may separate algorithm construction, performance analysis, and resource guarantees; lower-bound routes may separate hard-family construction, oracle information limits, and their conversion into the required bound.

The Brain interprets findings from independent algorithmic and hardness investigations in relation to the current targets and proof obligations. The selected subproblems 𝒬r\mathcal{Q}_{r} form a versioned batch. Each assignment states its assumptions, target, dependencies, and completion criterion, which the Cell checks before starting. The Brain corrects any specification defect. Once accepted, the assignment’s mathematical scope remains fixed for the round; substantive revisions are issued by the Brain after round integration.

Candidate and incomplete results remain in the associated research records until an applicable argument supports their use in the boundaries.

Each Cell iteration ends with a local audit, an updated draft and working memory, and a checkpoint report. Incorporating a report from any Cell advances the shared state from tt to t+1t+1. If it adds supported bounds L+,U+L^{+},U^{+} on 𝒟+\mathcal{D}^{+} while existing evidence remains valid, then

Ls(t+1)(η)=max{Ls(t)(η),L+(η)},Us(t+1)(η)=min{Us(t)(η),U+(η)},η∈𝒟+.\displaystyle L_{s}^{(t+1)}(\eta)=\max\{L_{s}^{(t)}(\eta),L^{+}(\eta)\},\quad U_{s}^{(t+1)}(\eta)=\min\{U_{s}^{(t)}(\eta),U^{+}(\eta)\},\quad\eta\in\mathcal{D}^{+}. (4)

Only supported sides and validity domains are updated. If review reveals a gap in an argument, its status is revised and the affected boundary is recomputed from the remaining supported evidence.

Every checkpoint also updates the associated research records and the Brain’s short-term programme memory, including changed conclusions, route assessments, and proof dependencies. These updates occur even when the supported boundaries are unchanged. Cells pursue their accepted assignments independently. At each Cell’s checkpoint, the Brain uses the latest bracket and programme memory to return CONTINUE, PAUSE, or STEER, with any guidance confined to that assignment’s scope. A Cell may be paused when its intended contribution has already been established or further work is no longer needed for the programme’s remaining objectives. Substantive task revisions follow round integration.

2.2.3  Round Integration and Targeted Replanning

Once all Cells have completed their assignments, been paused, or exhausted their allocated iterations, the Brain integrates the batch’s findings with the Live Complexity Bracket and programme memory. It then assesses the declared resolution target. For finite positive supported bounds,

Us(t)≲𝒟Ls(t)⟹Ns⋆=Θ𝒟(Ls(t))=Θ𝒟(Us(t)).U_{s}^{(t)}\lesssim_{\mathcal{D}}L_{s}^{(t)}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad N_{s}^{\star}=\Theta_{\mathcal{D}}(L_{s}^{(t)})=\Theta_{\mathcal{D}}(U_{s}^{(t)}).

Specified logarithmic allowances use the corresponding O~\widetilde{O} and Θ~\widetilde{\Theta} relations; any stronger requirement is checked in addition. If the target remains unmet, the Brain recomputes 𝒢s(t)\mathcal{G}_{s}^{(t)} from the integrated bracket and selects the remaining regimes to pursue. Each new route aa has a target Hr+1,aH_{r+1,a} on a domain 𝒟r+1,atar\mathcal{D}_{r+1,a}^{\mathrm{tar}} contained in a regime of 𝒢s(t)\mathcal{G}_{s}^{(t)}. The Brain reconstructs the route’s obligations 𝒲r+1,a\mathcal{W}_{r+1,a}, revising or replacing components contradicted by the accumulated evidence. The revised obligations are separated into supported components and remaining work, with support assessed under the target’s assumptions, constructions, and quantifiers:

𝒲r+1,asupp={P∈𝒲r+1,a:P​ is supported in the integrated recordon ​𝒟r+1,atar},𝒲r+1,aopen=𝒲r+1,a∖𝒲r+1,asupp.\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{r+1,a}^{\mathrm{supp}}=\left\{P\in\mathcal{W}_{r+1,a}:\begin{array}[]{l}P\text{ is supported in the integrated record}\\ \text{on }\mathcal{D}_{r+1,a}^{\mathrm{tar}}\end{array}\right\},\quad\mathcal{W}_{r+1,a}^{\mathrm{open}}=\mathcal{W}_{r+1,a}\setminus\mathcal{W}_{r+1,a}^{\mathrm{supp}}.

The intended completion of each revised route and the next batch of subproblems are

(⋀P∈𝒲r+1,asuppP)∧(⋀P∈𝒲r+1,aopenP)⟹Hr+1,a,𝒬r+1⊆⋃a=1mr+1𝒲r+1,aopen.\displaystyle\left(\bigwedge_{P\in\mathcal{W}_{r+1,a}^{\mathrm{supp}}}P\right)\land\left(\bigwedge_{P\in\mathcal{W}_{r+1,a}^{\mathrm{open}}}P\right)\Longrightarrow H_{r+1,a},\quad\mathcal{Q}_{r+1}\subseteq\bigcup_{a=1}^{m_{r+1}}\mathcal{W}_{r+1,a}^{\mathrm{open}}. (5)

Any unproved composition step remains among the open obligations. The Brain packages the selected work as independent assignments with explicit premises and completion criteria. Because the targets and routes are reconstructed from the integrated findings, new obstructions can change the next batch even when the supported boundaries are unchanged.

2.2.4  Natural-Language Synthesis and Independent Review

When Round Integration indicates that the declared Complexity Bracket objective has been reached, the Brain merges the relevant Cell drafts into a unified natural-language result package. The package may contain an algorithm, hard construction, counterexample, theorem, or combination of these objects, together with the arguments required to establish the claimed update to the bracket. The Brain reconciles notation, aligns assumptions and parameter regimes, resolves dependencies among Cell results, and distinguishes internally established claims from external inputs and remaining conjectures.

The resulting package is evaluated by independent LLM reviewers that did not produce the underlying argument. Review examines the correctness and scope of the main statements, the consistency of assumptions and quantifiers, the closure of proof dependencies, the validity of transfers between settings, the coverage of relevant parameter regimes, and potential counterexamples. A review may accept the package, request a local correction, or determine that the programme remains mathematically incomplete.

Local presentation or derivation issues may be repaired by the Brain and reviewed again. A substantive proof gap, false claim, unsupported transfer, or missing regime is incorporated into the Live Complexity Bracket and triggers a new research round, with the review findings serving as additional evidence for targeted replanning.

A package that passes independent natural-language review proceeds to Formal Certification. Findings from Lean formalization or semantic-alignment review are returned to the Brain in structured form. The Brain may correct the statement or proof locally when the issue is limited, or reopen the research programme when certification exposes a deeper mathematical defect. Only after formal certification succeeds are the resulting claims admitted to Scientific Memory and passed to Manuscript Synthesis.

2.3  Cells

A Cell is the basic problem-solving unit of Colombo. Each Cell addresses a research subproblem assigned by the Brain. Starting from this assignment, it develops a candidate result, such as a proof or construction, submits its work to the Verifier, and refines it in response to the review. It then returns its findings, supporting evidence, and any unresolved obstacles to the Brain, informing the next round of research. The Brain dynamically selects and organizes four types of Cells according to the evolving needs of the research programme: upper-bound specialists develop algorithms and establish performance guarantees; lower-bound specialists construct hard instances and prove complexity lower bounds; experiment specialists probe conjectures and candidate constructions computationally; and general-purpose Cells play an undifferentiated role, exploring subproblems that do not yet call for a particular specialization and taking on a more specialized focus as needed.

2.3.1  Assignment and Differentiation

A Cell differentiates according to the scientific function required by the Brain’s current research programme. The Brain supplies a versioned subproblem that specifies the target, assumptions, relevant parameter regimes, and criteria for completion, together with the context needed to begin the investigation and its intended contribution to the Complexity Bracket. It configures the Cell as an upper-bound specialist, a lower-bound specialist, an experiment specialist, or a general-purpose Cell. This specialization directs the Cell’s attention toward algorithmic guarantees, hardness mechanisms, computational investigation, or broader exploration, respectively.

All Cell types share a common repertoire of internal research roles. Differentiation determines their emphasis and initial organization, while the Cell adapts its methods as the investigation develops. On receiving an assignment, the Cell checks that its objects, assumptions, and objectives are sufficiently specified. Within this scope, it can formulate auxiliary conjectures, decompose arguments, and pursue alternative approaches. Discoveries that require changing the assigned assumptions or scope are returned to the Brain as proposals for further research.

2.3.2  Collaborative Problem Solving

Collaborative problem solving combines four complementary agent roles. The prove agent develops proofs, reductions, and mathematical constructions. The disprove agent challenges candidate claims and searches for counterexamples or weaknesses in proposed mechanisms. The experiment agent designs and executes computational investigations that test conjectures, examine boundary cases, and reveal patterns. The explore agent investigates relevant literature, related settings, and alternative formulations, identifying results and techniques whose applicability can be assessed within the current assignment.

These roles contribute to a common investigation through repeated exchanges of conjectures, arguments, and evidence. A computational anomaly may motivate an exact counterexample; that counterexample may expose a missing condition and suggest a revised construction. An imported technique may supply an intermediate lemma that connects two previously separate parts of an argument. The sequence and combination of agents depend on what the Cell currently needs to understand. The orchestrate agent directs this evolving collaboration, selecting the next investigations in response to their mathematical consequences.

2.3.3  Adaptive Orchestration

The orchestrate agent maintains the Cell’s local research strategy. Its working state identifies the assigned target, candidate approaches, available results, and unresolved obligations. From this state, it formulates tasks for the investigative agents, supplies the relevant context, and determines which tasks can proceed concurrently. Parallel investigations may pursue distinct proof mechanisms, address separable obligations, or challenge a candidate result from different directions.

As contributions return, the orchestrator interprets their consequences for the current approaches. A proved intermediate claim may enable the next step of an argument; a refuted conjecture may require revising or abandoning a route; an inconclusive experiment may suggest a more discriminating test. The orchestrator combines compatible contributions, preserves useful results from unsuccessful attempts, and updates the remaining obligations. Its next decisions follow this revised mathematical state, including whether to deepen an approach, change methods, request verification, or return a progress report.

This local control allows the Cell to reorganize its agents throughout an assignment. Resources can be redirected toward obligations that determine the viability of a route or findings that distinguish competing explanations. The Brain retains responsibility for the broader programme and for changes to the assignment itself. The Cell’s orchestrator provides the focused reasoning and coordination needed to advance that assignment.

2.3.4  Communication and Research Records

Agents communicate through task instructions, questions, result submissions, and review feedback, with references to a shared Cell Workspace. Each contribution identifies the mathematical objects it concerns and the assumptions under which it applies. The orchestrator assembles the context needed for each task from this workspace, allowing successive agents to continue an investigation while preserving the provenance of its results.

The workspace organizes mathematical content around four related objects. A Claim states an assertion under explicit assumptions; an Argument supplies a proof, refutation, or reduction concerning that assertion; an Attempt records the investigation of a particular route; and a Gap identifies an unresolved obligation within a specific argument. Examples, experiments, sources, and review findings are linked to the objects they support or challenge. This structure preserves the distinction between a statement, the evidence concerning it, and its role in an ongoing investigation. Revisions retain these relationships, so that agents can identify which statements and dependencies a result actually addresses.

Model Context Protocol (MCP) interfaces provide access to the research tools and resources used by the agents, including services for retrieving records, consulting sources, and executing computations. The Cell’s communication conventions specify how returned material is associated with tasks and incorporated into the research record. A concise working state supports immediate orchestration, while the underlying arguments and attempt histories remain available for inspection and reuse.

2.3.5  Verification and Revision

Verification accompanies local inquiry at both intermediate and reporting stages. The Verifier examines whether a submitted argument or body of evidence supports its stated conclusion under the assigned assumptions. Its checks cover mathematical validity, the applicability of imported results, the consistency of dependencies, and the scope of any experimental findings. Verification also applies to refutations: a proposed counterexample must satisfy the claim’s assumptions and contradict its conclusion. The disprove agent contributes adversarial investigation, while the Verifier independently assesses the evidence produced by that investigation and the other agents.

Review findings return to the orchestrator as specific issues to resolve. These may lead to repairing a derivation, testing a construction more carefully, revisiting a dependency, or reconsidering the current route. Review status remains associated with the versions and dependencies actually examined. When the Cell assembles a complete argument, the Verifier also checks the connections between its components, including any new inferences introduced during integration. Completion requires a reviewed resolution of the assigned target with its actual dependencies satisfied; obligations belonging only to abandoned routes remain part of the historical record. Natural-language review and formal machine checking retain their distinct evidentiary status.

2.3.6  Feedback to the Brain

At reporting checkpoints, the Cell consolidates its progress into a Cell Report. The report identifies the assignment and presents the current conclusions, supporting arguments or evidence, review findings, and remaining obligations. It also preserves reusable intermediate results and explains why particular approaches stalled or failed. Partial progress, a refuted target, or a specification issue can each provide a substantive return to the Brain. Execution states, such as a pause or exhausted budget, are recorded separately from these mathematical outcomes.

The Brain interprets these reports in relation to the current Complexity Bracket and the results of other Cells. A supported improvement can narrow the bracket within its established regime, while a counterexample or diagnosed obstacle can change the working conjecture and research priorities. The Brain then revises the programme and selects or reorganizes Cells for the next round. Reusable arguments, constructions, and diagnoses can also inform Scientific Memory. Through this repeated exchange, local investigations contribute both mathematical advances and a progressively clearer account of what the programme should investigate next.

2.4  Formal Certification

Formal Certification translates independently reviewed mathematical arguments into machine-checked proofs in Lean. The Brain provides a Formalization Package containing the versioned claims, normalized definitions, proof dependencies, and supporting arguments. These are organized into modular proof obligations and formalized under a pinned Lean toolchain. The resulting proof terms are checked by the Lean kernel, with explicit accounting for axioms and external dependencies; unresolved placeholders or unsupported custom axioms prevent certification.

Certification combines kernel checking with semantic alignment: each formal statement is compared with the research claim it is intended to establish, including its assumptions, quantifiers, parameter regimes, and conclusion. The findings return to the Brain and enter Short-Term Memory, where they guide corrections or further Cell assignments. A revised statement retains an explicit relationship to the original claim and is assessed within its revised scope. An incomplete formalization remains an unresolved obligation.

Successful certification produces a package of certified results linking the mathematical statement to its Lean declarations, proof artifacts, dependencies, and the associated algorithms or hard constructions. The package is retained in Long-Term Memory as a certified result and supplied to the Paper Composer. Its precise scope determines which bounds or setting relations it can support in the Complexity Atlas.

2.5  Paper Composer

The Paper Composer transforms fully verified Lean proofs into complete research papers. It develops the introduction and related work, articulates the contributions, and compares the new rates with prior results under aligned assumptions, oracle models, parameter regimes, and success criteria. These comparisons make improvements, matching or near-optimal bounds, and remaining gaps explicit.

The certified results are presented through clear theorem statements, proof overviews, and complete arguments, supported by algorithm descriptions, examples, and figures. Using its built-in experimental capabilities, the Paper Composer designs and runs supplementary experiments to illustrate predicted scaling, compare relevant algorithms, or examine behavior at finite problem sizes. These experiments are reported with reproducible procedures and clearly stated limitations.

Finally, it integrates these materials with the abstract, discussion, references, and appendices into a coherent manuscript. Iterative review and revision refine the mathematical exposition, literature comparisons, experimental reporting, and overall presentation, producing a publication-ready paper with complete proofs and reproducible supporting materials.

2.6  Memory

Memory in Colombo operates at two complementary time scales. Short-Term Memory maintains the state of an active research programme, while Long-Term Memory preserves reusable knowledge and research experience across programmes. At both time scales, records retain their assumptions, dependencies, provenance, and evidence status. Their exchange allows ongoing work to draw on earlier investigations and contribute new results and experience to future research.

2.6.1  Short-Term Memory

Short-Term Memory supports the decisions required to advance an active programme. At the Brain level, it contains the Setting Profile, research plan, working conjectures, versioned assignments, Live Complexity Bracket, round history, and review feedback. It records the evidence motivating important decisions, including why a route was pursued, redirected, or abandoned. This state provides continuity across research rounds and supplies the context for targeted replanning.

At the Cell level, Short-Term Memory is maintained through the Cell Workspace. Its Claims, Arguments, Attempts, and Gaps capture the current investigation, together with experimental records, sources, and verification findings. The Cell’s orchestrator uses this record to prepare agent tasks and integrate their outputs; checkpoint reports make the relevant progress available to the Brain. Cells update their own workspaces and designated evidence channels, while the Brain maintains the programme-level state and controls assignment revisions.

Short-Term Memory is scoped to current research activity. Its records remain versioned and available for later inspection, while selected results and research experience are consolidated into Long-Term Memory with links to their original context.

2.6.2  Long-Term Memory

Long-Term Memory supports knowledge reuse across settings and research programmes. Its principal stores are the Complexity Atlas, the Theorem Library, the Algorithm Library, and the Hard-Family Library. The Atlas records settings, their relations, and Complexity Brackets together with the sources and evidence status of the constituent bounds. The theorem library preserves claim-level certification artifacts. The algorithm and hard-family libraries retain constructions together with their assumptions, guarantees, relevant oracle and algorithm classes, and conditions for transfer. The Atlas stores 𝒫s=(𝖲s,ℬs,ℰs)\mathcal{P}_{s}=(\mathsf{S}_{s},\mathcal{B}_{s},\mathcal{E}_{s}) for each setting. Certified programme results update the applicable bounds and their evidence; provisional research records retain their own status in Scientific Memory rather than entering the supported bracket automatically. A subsequent programme receives the current Profile as a new input snapshot 𝒫sin\mathcal{P}_{s}^{\mathrm{in}}.

The Algorithm Library and Hard-Family Library retain not only constructions but also the properties that explain their effectiveness or limitations, together with the evidence and applicability conditions supporting those explanations. These linked records support the reciprocal investigations and formation of new settings described in Section 2.7.2.

Long-Term Memory also retains useful partial results, counterexamples, proof techniques, failed attempts, and methodological lessons. These entries preserve the arguments or observations supporting them and the limitations of their conclusions. A failed search can inform future strategy while retaining its status as an inconclusive attempt; an established impossibility result is recorded as a claim with its own supporting argument and verification status. This organization makes research experience reusable without losing the distinctions required for mathematical reasoning.

The Sensorium draws on Long-Term Memory to identify unresolved settings, recurring mechanisms, and promising extensions. The Brain retrieves relevant results and experience into Short-Term Memory when planning a programme, and Cells consult the material needed for their assignments. New certified results and selected research records are subsequently consolidated back into Long-Term Memory. Through this exchange, each programme can refine the Complexity Atlas and expand the mathematical resources available to the next.

2.7  Research Mechanisms

Self-Organization and Adversarial Co-Ascent connect the system’s components into an adaptive research process. The former organizes inquiry across scales; the latter makes algorithmic and hardness investigations inform one another.

2.7.1  Self-Organization

Self-Organization structures and directs frontier-to-frontier research by making the evolving frontier both the basis for organizing inquiry and an object revised by its outcomes.

Frontier-guided research planning.

The Sensorium uses Setting Profiles 𝒫s=(𝖲s,ℬs,ℰs)\mathcal{P}_{s}=(\mathsf{S}_{s},\mathcal{B}_{s},\mathcal{E}_{s}) and their relations in the Atlas to identify promising research directions. A selected input Profile 𝒫sin\mathcal{P}_{s}^{\mathrm{in}} initializes a programme at t=0t=0, as specified in Eq. (3). In research round rr, the Brain draws on reasoning, search, experiments, and memory to conjecture optimal rates and develop targets Hr,aH_{r,a} for routes a=1,…,mra=1,\ldots,m_{r} addressing the unresolved regimes 𝒢s(t)\mathcal{G}_{s}^{(t)}. The decomposition in Eq. (2) turns the required obligations 𝒲r,a\mathcal{W}_{r,a} into Cell assignments 𝒬r\mathcal{Q}_{r}. The frontier determines what needs to be advanced; the proposed routes determine how the necessary research is organized.

Evidence-driven reorganization.

The shared state incorporates findings from independently running Cells. When new supported bounds are added and existing evidence remains valid, Eq. (4) implies ℬs(t+1)​(η)⊆ℬs(t)​(η)\mathcal{B}_{s}^{(t+1)}(\eta)\subseteq\mathcal{B}_{s}^{(t)}(\eta) (η∈𝒟+)(\eta\in\mathcal{D}^{+}) on the new result’s proven domain 𝒟+\mathcal{D}^{+}. Findings also affect research organization without changing the boundaries: a proved component can enable a route, a counterexample can undermine it, and a partial argument can isolate the remaining obstacle. The Brain uses these findings to assess which investigations should continue and where guidance is needed. Round integration then revises the targets and unresolved obligations 𝒲r+1,aopen\mathcal{W}_{r+1,a}^{\mathrm{open}} from which 𝒬r+1\mathcal{Q}_{r+1} is formed, as specified in Eq. (5). Successive rounds are consequently organized around the current gap and the evidence available to address it.

Frontier renewal.

After review and certification, accepted claims revise the applicable Atlas bounds ℬs\mathcal{B}_{s} and evidence ℰs\mathcal{E}_{s}, while Scientific Memory retains methods, mechanisms, and research experience with their applicability conditions and evidence status. The Sensorium uses the revised Profiles to reassess known settings and characterize new ones. Resolving a gap changes which questions merit attention; discovering a reusable mechanism changes which investigations become feasible. Subsequent programmes receive the current Profiles as new input snapshots and draw on the accumulated scientific resources.

2.7.2  Adversarial Co-Ascent

Adversarial Co-Ascent seeks more efficient algorithms and stronger hard-instance constructions through reciprocal challenge. By identifying what enables algorithms to succeed and what makes problem families difficult, it turns these interactions into improved complexity bounds and new research questions.

Reciprocal challenge.

Fix the specification 𝖲s\mathsf{S}_{s} and parameters η=(ε,δ,θ)\eta=(\varepsilon,\delta,\theta). Given a candidate family ∅≠ℋ⊆ℐs​(θ)\varnothing\neq\mathcal{H}\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{s}(\theta), the algorithmic direction seeks a method that solves it with fewer resources. Given a candidate algorithm A∈𝒜sA\in\mathcal{A}_{s}, the hardness direction seeks instances that expose its limitations. The two search objectives are

Against family ℋ:infA′∈𝒜ssupI∈ℋNs(A′,I;η);Against algorithm A:supI∈ℐs​(θ)Ns(A,I;η).\displaystyle\text{Against family }\mathcal{H}:\ \inf_{A^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}_{s}}\sup_{I\in\mathcal{H}}N_{s}(A^{\prime},I;\eta);\quad\text{Against algorithm }A:\ \sup_{I\in\mathcal{I}_{s}(\theta)}N_{s}(A,I;\eta).

Solving the entire family below its proposed lower bound exposes exploitable structure; a counterexample to an algorithm’s guarantee reveals a limitation of its information use. The system analyzes these outcomes to guide revised algorithms and hard constructions. For each target Hr,aH_{r,a}, the obligations 𝒲r,a\mathcal{W}_{r,a} state the properties needed to justify the proposed improvement and guide further construction and challenge.

Improving complexity bounds.

Within the selected setting, these investigations seek an algorithm A+∈𝒜sA^{+}\in\mathcal{A}_{s} and a family ∅≠ℋ+⊆ℐs​(θ)\varnothing\neq\mathcal{H}^{+}\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{s}(\theta) supporting bounds of the form

L+(η)≤infA′∈𝒜ssupI∈ℋ+Ns(A′,I;η)≤Ns⋆(η),Ns⋆(η)≤supI∈ℐs​(θ)Ns(A+,I;η)≤U+(η).\displaystyle L^{+}(\eta)\leq\inf_{A^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}_{s}}\sup_{I\in\mathcal{H}^{+}}N_{s}(A^{\prime},I;\eta)\leq N_{s}^{\star}(\eta),\quad N_{s}^{\star}(\eta)\leq\sup_{I\in\mathcal{I}_{s}(\theta)}N_{s}(A^{+},I;\eta)\leq U^{+}(\eta).

The upper guarantee must cover the full model class, and the lower bound must cover every admissible algorithm; tests against selected candidates alone do not establish either claim. All bounds are proved uniformly over their declared parameter regimes. Applicable improvements tighten ℬs(t)\mathcal{B}_{s}^{(t)} through Eq. (4). Matching bounds identify the optimal rate; matching up to the declared logarithmic factors establishes near-optimality.

Discovering new questions.

The same interactions can reveal structural properties that distinguish an easier subclass or sustain a hardness mechanism. Abstracting these properties into explicit assumptions can motivate a new specification 𝖲s′\mathsf{S}_{s^{\prime}} and Setting Profile 𝒫s′\mathcal{P}_{s^{\prime}}. The Sensorium characterizes the resulting questions, whose complexity requires separate investigation. Scientific Memory retains the constructions, structural insights, and supporting evidence with their validation status. Co-ascent thereby sharpens the current frontier while supplying new questions and methods for subsequent research. Figure 3(b) illustrates the reciprocal interaction between algorithm design and hardness construction. Each side exposes mechanisms and limitations that guide the next refinement of the other.

3  Research Outcomes

The architecture described above supports research across related oracle-complexity settings. Table 1 summarizes the current portfolio of 56 research works across six task classes: single-objective optimization, bilevel optimization, minimax and saddle-point problems, variational inequalities, matrix computation, and online learning and bandits. Across these tasks, the information models include zeroth-order value evaluations, first-order gradient access, second- and higher-order derivative access, and specialized problem-dependent oracles. The selected research programmes below illustrate how Colombo advances the Complexity Atlas through algorithmic advances, hardness results, and characterizations of the costs imposed by information access and problem structure. Detailed historical comparisons and complexity bounds are collected in Appendix A; each comparison retains its oracle model, success criterion, and parameter regime.

The subsections below cite representative papers already available on arXiv, alongside related ongoing studies. The complete collection of 56 papers and a demonstration of the Colombo system will be made available through the following webpages:

    Project website: under construction.

  • •

    System demo: under construction.

3.1  Closing Long-Standing Gaps in Zeroth-Order Optimization

The intrinsic dimension cost of exact function-value access remained a fundamental open question for three decades. Following the upper bound of Protasov (1996), the additional dimension factor in convex zeroth-order complexity lacked a matching lower-bound explanation until the deterministic and randomized results of Kerger (2026) and Zhang et al. (2026l) in July 2026. Against this thirty-year backdrop, Colombo established new lower-bound milestones in smooth convex and stochastic nonconvex optimization.

To our knowledge, our September 16 paper (Wu et al., 2026e) gave the first matching exact-value lower bound for smooth convex optimization under deterministic bounded queries in the moderate-accuracy regime. The upper benchmark uses classical acceleration with coordinate finite differences; our paper supplies its bounded-query implementation, while the new complexity contribution is the lower bound. Our September 24 paper (Zhang et al., 2026d) established joint dimension–accuracy lower bounds for smooth stochastic nonconvex optimization in a bounded-domain setting. Queries and the output lie in a public ball XX, the initial gap satisfies the local budget f⁡(x0)−minx∈X⁡f⁡(x)≤ΔXf(x_{0})-\min_{x\in X}f(x)\leq\Delta_{X}, and a stationary point is guaranteed inside XX. The lower bound is Ω⁡(d​H​L02​ΔX/ε4)\Omega(dHL_{0}^{2}\Delta_{X}/\varepsilon^{4}) on a constructed ball of radius Θ⁡(ΔX/ε)\Theta(\Delta_{X}/\varepsilon), allowing arbitrary adaptive randomization and sample reuse.

These initial lower-bound results were followed within weeks by complementary advances under unrestricted queries. Dorn et al. (2026), whose preprint was submitted on September 29, established matching smooth-convex bounds for randomized algorithms over a wider accuracy range. In their October 14 preprint, Xia and Yuan (2026) study a different smooth nonconvex setting: queries and the output may lie anywhere in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, while the objective is globally lower bounded with f⁡(x0)−infℝdf≤Δf(x_{0})-\inf_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}f\leq\Delta. Their reusable-sample lower bound is Ω⁡(d​L02​min⁡{H​Δ,L02}/ε4)\Omega(dL_{0}^{2}\min\{H\Delta,L_{0}^{2}\}/\varepsilon^{4}) under their stated dimension and accuracy conditions; it has the full H​ΔH\Delta dependence when H​Δ≤L02H\Delta\leq L_{0}^{2}. Both studies assume a globally smooth population objective, but the spatial access and gap assumptions differ. Table A.1 records these developments with their respective settings.

Colombo also establishes, to our knowledge, the first uniform, all-dimensional characterization of exact-value complexity for nonsmooth strongly convex optimization (Anonymous Authors, 2026). Its upper and lower bounds match up to logarithmic factors and remain uniform in the nearly degenerate regime L↓μ​RL\downarrow\mu R.

For nonsmooth convex finite sums, existing two-point methods already achieve O⁡(d​L2​R2/ε2)O(dL^{2}R^{2}/\varepsilon^{2}) individual function-value queries by uniformly sampling a client and querying that same client’s function at two points. This benchmark follows from Shamir (2017) and is also attained, up to logarithmic factors, by the incremental finite-sum framework of Gasnikov et al. (2022) and the stochastic federated framework of Lobanov et al. (2023). Wei et al. (2023) directly study fixed client losses: with communication every step, their Theorem 2.3 yields O⁡(N​d2​L2​R2/ε2)O(Nd^{2}L^{2}R^{2}/\varepsilon^{2}) total queries after tuning, using Gaussian perturbations with full-space access.

Our contribution is a finite-population localization algorithm (Zhang et al., 2026i) with cost O~​(d2+d​N)\widetilde{O}(d^{2}+dN). It improves the high-accuracy O~​(N​d2)\widetilde{O}(Nd^{2}) baseline obtained by applying the value-only localization method of Protasov (1996) to the aggregate objective, where each aggregate value costs NN client queries. Combining our algorithm with the existing two-point method and our matching client-dependent lower bounds gives

Θ~​(min⁡{d​L2​R2ε2,d2+d​N})\widetilde{\Theta}\!\left(\min\!\left\{\frac{dL^{2}R^{2}}{\varepsilon^{2}},\ d^{2}+dN\right\}\right)

for adaptive randomized selected-client queries confined to the feasible ball, in the theorem’s stated dimension and accuracy regime. Table A.1 distinguishes the query domains and oracle simulations underlying these comparisons.

3.2  Resolving Randomized First-Order Complexity Gaps

Two autoresearch studies conducted with Colombo settle the optimal accuracy exponents of randomized first-order nonconvex optimization under fixed finite-order smoothness of order p≥2p\geq 2. The task is to find xx satisfying ‖∇f​(x)‖≤ε\|\nabla f(x)\|\leq\varepsilon using only exact function values and gradients, even when higher-order smoothness is available. Let Δ\Delta bound the initial objective gap and LqL_{q} bound the Lipschitz constant of the qqth derivative. We consider the worst case over finite dimensions and allow unrestricted adaptive randomized algorithms with constant success probability.

The historical progression is summarized in Table A.3. With the initial-gap and derivative-Lipschitz budgets normalized to one, Carmon et al. (2017) obtained deterministic upper bounds of O(ε−7/4log(1/ε))O(\varepsilon^{-7/4}\log(1/\varepsilon)) under Lipschitz Hessians and O(ε−5/3log(1/ε))O(\varepsilon^{-5/3}\log(1/\varepsilon)) under Lipschitz third derivatives in 2017. Their subsequent lower-bound study (Carmon et al., 2021), first released in November 2017, established deterministic bounds of Ω(ε−12/7)\Omega(\varepsilon^{-12/7}) and Ωp(ε−8/5)\Omega_{p}(\varepsilon^{-8/5}), respectively, leaving both rates unmatched. Li and Lin (2023) subsequently removed the logarithmic factor from the Hessian-Lipschitz upper bound, and Zhou (2026a) established matching deterministic lower bounds of Ω(ε−7/4)\Omega(\varepsilon^{-7/4}) and Ωp(ε−5/3)\Omega_{p}(\varepsilon^{-5/3}) in 2026. These advances left open whether randomization could improve the rates.

Our Hessian-Lipschitz result (Zhang et al., 2026e) closes this randomized gap with a lower bound that matches the deterministic upper bound in all problem parameters. In the stated high-accuracy regime, the minimax query complexity is

Qrand(ε)=Θ(ΔL11/2L21/4ε−7/4).Q_{\mathrm{rand}}(\varepsilon)=\Theta\!\left(\Delta L_{1}^{1/2}L_{2}^{1/4}\varepsilon^{-7/4}\right).

Our higher-order result (Zhang et al., 2026k) establishes, for every fixed finite p≥3p\geq 3 and simultaneous budgets Δ≤1\Delta\leq 1 and Lq≤1L_{q}\leq 1 for 1≤q≤p1\leq q\leq p,

Ωp(ε−5/3)≤Qp,rand(ε)≤Op(ε−5/3log(2/ε)).\Omega_{p}(\varepsilon^{-5/3})\;\leq\;Q_{p,\mathrm{rand}}(\varepsilon)\;\leq\;O_{p}\!\left(\varepsilon^{-5/3}\log(2/\varepsilon)\right).

The upper bound follows from the existing deterministic algorithm of Carmon et al. (2017). For every fixed p≥4p\geq 4, Zhou et al. (2026) established a randomized gradient-only lower bound of Ωp​(ε−(3/2+1/(2​p)))\Omega_{p}(\varepsilon^{-(3/2+1/(2p))}) under simultaneous first- and ppth-order smoothness budgets. Our lower bound reaches Ωp(ε−5/3)\Omega_{p}(\varepsilon^{-5/3}) even when exact function values are also available, under the stated simultaneous derivative budgets. For p=3p=3, it establishes the same accuracy rate with this richer value-and-gradient oracle. Together, the two studies characterize randomized first-order complexity as Θ(ε−7/4)\Theta(\varepsilon^{-7/4}) under Lipschitz Hessians and Θ~p(ε−5/3)\widetilde{\Theta}_{p}(\varepsilon^{-5/3}) for every fixed finite p≥3p\geq 3 under normalized budgets: additional finite-order smoothness cannot improve the polynomial dependence beyond ε−5/3\varepsilon^{-5/3}.

3.3  Closing Oracle-Complexity Gaps for Variational Inequalities

Four Colombo studies characterize complementary VI complexity limits (Table A.4). For every fixed p≥2p\geq 2, we develop a new deterministic higher-order algorithm (Zhang et al., 2026b) for general smooth monotone VIs, reducing query complexity from O~p(ε−1/p)\widetilde{O}_{p}(\varepsilon^{-1/p}) (Chen et al., 2026d) to O~p(ε−2/(3p−1))\widetilde{O}_{p}(\varepsilon^{-2/(3p-1)}) at fixed smoothness and geometry. The algorithm combines extrapolated Halpern iteration with a finite hierarchy of certified solvers and returns an explicit tangent-residual certificate. We also prove an Ωp(ε−2/(3p−1))\Omega_{p}(\varepsilon^{-2/(3p-1)}) lower bound against unrestricted adaptive randomized algorithms, establishing optimality up to logarithmic factors. For scalar convex–concave problems, the new VI algorithm improves the upper bound from O~p(ε−4/(3p+1))\widetilde{O}_{p}(\varepsilon^{-4/(3p+1)}) (Chen et al., 2026c) to O~p(ε−2/(3p−1))\widetilde{O}_{p}(\varepsilon^{-2/(3p-1)}); a separate Colombo study (Li et al., 2026) removes the tensor restrictions from the matching lower bound. Combined with the logarithm-free algorithm of Zhang et al. (2026m), our lower bounds yield Θp(ε−2/(3p−1))\Theta_{p}(\varepsilon^{-2/(3p-1)}) complexity for both settings at fixed smoothness and geometry.

For strongly monotone VIs, Colombo (Zhang et al., 2026g) improves the certified tensor baseline’s polynomial condition dependence from O~p​(κD2/(p+1))\widetilde{O}_{p}(\kappa_{D}^{2/(p+1)}) to O~p​(κD2/(3​p−1))\widetilde{O}_{p}(\kappa_{D}^{2/(3p-1)}) and proves a matching lower bound up to logarithms, where κD=Lp​Dp−1/μ\kappa_{D}=L_{p}D^{p-1}/\mu. For stochastic weak-Minty root finding, we establish matching Θ⁡(ε−4)\Theta(\varepsilon^{-4}) expected-sample complexity at fixed positive noise variance, including algorithms with random stopping (Colombo, ). This result assumes fresh conditionally unbiased, bounded-variance observations and ρ​L≤1/4\rho L\leq 1/4. Its upper bound is a two-batch specialization of the damped extragradient method of Diakonikolas et al. (2021); our new result is the unrestricted lower bound for expected sample cost.

3.4  Sharp Complexity Limits for Stochastic Bilevel Optimization

Two Colombo studies establish sharp accuracy limits for nonconvex–strongly-convex bilevel optimization using fresh, globally unbiased first-order samples. Our accuracy study (Zhang et al., 2026h) independently establishes the Ω⁡(ε−6)\Omega(\varepsilon^{-6}) barrier for arbitrary randomized adaptive algorithms and quantifies its dependence on conditioning and lower Hessian variation. In the common-scale regime, the leading lower bound is Ω⁡(κ10​ε−6)\Omega(\kappa^{10}\varepsilon^{-6}), against the existing O~​(κ11​ε−6)\widetilde{O}(\kappa^{11}\varepsilon^{-6}) upper benchmark of Chen et al. (2025). Earlier Ω⁡(ε−6)\Omega(\varepsilon^{-6}) bounds of Kwon et al. (2024) use a y∗y^{*}-aware oracle; our study addresses globally unbiased samples throughout the domain. Thus the accuracy exponent is settled, with one conditioning factor remaining; our variation-sensitive upper analysis also gives matching leading rates in the specified curvature-controlled and small-gap regimes.

Our smoothness study (Wu et al., 2026d) establishes Θp​(ε−4−2/p)\Theta_{p}(\varepsilon^{-4-2/p}) for every fixed finite smoothness order p≥1p\geq 1. Beyond fixed-order exponents, it determines how increasing smoothness improves complexity under derivative budgets Lj=M​Λj​(j!)βL_{j}=M\Lambda^{j}(j!)^{\beta}:

Qp,β∗(ε)=Θ(ε−4𝒟p,β(ε)2),𝒟p,β(ε)=infr∈ℕ1≤r≤prβε−1/r.Q^{*}_{p,\beta}(\varepsilon)=\Theta\!\left(\varepsilon^{-4}\mathcal{D}_{p,\beta}(\varepsilon)^{2}\right),\qquad\mathcal{D}_{p,\beta}(\varepsilon)=\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}r\in\mathbb{N}\\ 1\leq r\leq p\end{subarray}}r^{\beta}\varepsilon^{-1/r}.

The constants are independent of pp, including p=∞p=\infty. This yields Θ⁡(ε−4)\Theta(\varepsilon^{-4}) for an exponential derivative envelope (β=0\beta=0) and Θ⁡(ε−4​log2⁡(1/ε))\Theta(\varepsilon^{-4}\log^{2}(1/\varepsilon)) for an analytic envelope (β=1\beta=1), attained by a matching algorithm using independent gradient samples. Table A.5 places these contributions alongside earlier and concurrent results.

3.5  Sharp Oracle Complexity of Nonconvex Minimax Optimization

Five Colombo studies characterize the cost of finding stationary points of Φ⁡(x)=maxy⁡f⁡(x,y)\Phi(x)=\max_{y}f(x,y) when ff is nonconvex in xx and concave (NC–C) or strongly concave (NC–SC) in yy. Beginning with accelerated proximal methods in 2019–2020 (Thekumparampil et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2020), the literature established increasingly sharp upper bounds, while subsequent lower bounds often applied to linear-span or zero-respecting algorithms. Table A.6 traces how our studies resolve remaining gaps for unrestricted adaptive randomized methods in the stated oracle models and parameter regimes.

For fresh stochastic NC–SC optimization, Colombo (Wu et al., 2026c) establishes the necessity of linear condition-number dependence in the global stochastic cost, closing the earlier κ1/3\kappa^{1/3}-versus-κ\kappa gap; the linear-κ\kappa leading upper dependence was already available from SAPD+ (Zhang et al., 2022). Our matching characterization also identifies a separate κ2​σ2/ε2\kappa^{2}\sigma^{2}/\varepsilon^{2} statistical refinement cost and an additive logarithmic cost of dual initialization; without initialization control, no finite dimension-free bound exists. For NC–C optimization, we remove structural restrictions from exact and stochastic lower bounds (Zhang et al., 2026f) and match them using only an initial primal-gap bound, addressing the extension to arbitrary randomized algorithms explicitly left open by Wu et al. (2026a).

The finite-sum studies reveal how reusable component access changes these limits. For NC–C, Colombo (Wu et al., 2026b) determines the joint dependence on component count and dual diameter, including two transitions between three optimal regimes; its large-diameter upper branch recovers the earlier Catalyst rate (Yang et al., 2020). For NC–SC, we prove matching lower bounds (Zhang et al., 2026c) for unrestricted randomized component queries in the ill-conditioned regime. The upper analysis adapts the Catalyst–SVRG/SAGA benchmark of Zhang et al. (2021) to controlled dual initialization and a fixed query budget. Finally, our full-Hessian study (Zhang et al., 2026a) identifies three optimal regimes with leading accuracy dependence Θ~(ε−3/2)\widetilde{\Theta}(\varepsilon^{-3/2}), Θ~(ε−12/7)\widetilde{\Theta}(\varepsilon^{-12/7}), and Θ~​(ε−2)\widetilde{\Theta}(\varepsilon^{-2}). The full parameter factors and regime boundaries appear in Table A.6; matching holds when the leading term dominates initialization costs. These regimes specify when second-order information improves the classical first-order benchmark. Together, these results exhibit Colombo’s ability to develop related algorithms and lower bounds into systematic complexity characterizations.

3.6  Resolving Open Problems in Geometry and Matrix Computation

Colombo also resolved three concrete complexity questions in hyperbolic optimization, simplex-based matrix games, and low-rank approximation. These studies establish the necessary costs of curvature, randomized equilibrium computation, and simultaneous rank and accuracy requirements. In each case, the new lower bound matches an existing algorithmic upper bound, with the logarithmic qualifications recorded below.

Geodesically convex optimization in hyperbolic space.

The upper bound of Zhang and Sra (2016) left open whether the curvature factor ζ\zeta must multiply the entire accuracy cost ε−2\varepsilon^{-2}. Criscitiello and Boumal (2023) obtained the multiplicative Ω⁡(ζ​ε−2)\Omega(\zeta\varepsilon^{-2}) lower bound under geodesic-span and historical-halfspace restrictions, while their general lower bounds gave weaker curvature and accuracy dependence. Our result (Wu et al., 2026f) removes these algorithmic restrictions and establishes Ω⁡(ζ​ε−2)\Omega(\zeta\varepsilon^{-2}) for arbitrary adaptive deterministic first-order algorithms, determining the dimension-uniform complexity as Θ⁡(ζ​ε−2)\Theta(\zeta\varepsilon^{-2}) (Table A.9).

Simplex-based matrix games.

The classical O~​(ε−1)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-1}) matrix–vector query bound (Nemirovski, 2004) was improved in 2025 (Karmarkar et al., 2025) and then sharpened to O~(ε−2/3)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-2/3}) in 2026 (Karmarkar et al., 2026). Matching deterministic lower bounds left the power of randomization unresolved (Kornowski and Shamir, 2026). Our work (Wu and Fang, 2026) proves Ω~(ε−2/3)\widetilde{\Omega}(\varepsilon^{-2/3}) for arbitrary adaptive randomized algorithms in both ball–simplex and simplex–simplex games, establishing the optimal randomized accuracy exponent in the high-dimensional regime (Table A.9).

Low-rank matrix approximation.

Block Krylov methods established fast query upper bounds in 2015 (Musco and Musco, 2015), followed by sharper finite-Schatten-norm bounds in 2022 (Bakshi et al., 2022). The joint cost of rank and accuracy remained unresolved and was explicitly posed by Bakshi and Narayanan (2023). For the Frobenius norm, the previous general-rank lower frontier recorded by Amsel et al. (2026) was only additive, Ω(k+ε−1/3)\Omega(k+\varepsilon^{-1/3}). Our work (Zhang et al., 2026j) supplies the missing multiplicative rank dependence for arbitrary adaptive randomized algorithms, matching existing upper bounds up to logarithms for every fixed finite Schatten norm and the spectral norm (Table A.9). It also characterizes the polynomial transition between these regimes when the norm parameter grows.

4  Applications and Future Directions

Oracle-based optimization studies algorithm design and performance limits under prescribed information access and resource constraints. This section examines how Colombo’s research framework could be adapted to applied optimization, using GPU kernel autotuning to illustrate the construction and investigation of a candidate Setting Profile. We then consider extending Adversarial Co-Ascent to the joint development of training methods and diagnostic challenges, before outlining the longer-term vision of Autopoietic Science.

4.1  Applications of Oracle-Based Optimization

Applications of oracle-based optimization include large-scale model training, online decision-making, and engineering optimization based on simulations or hardware evaluation (Bottou et al., 2018; Lattimore and Szepesvári, 2020; Frazier, 2018). An oracle formulation makes the available information and its acquisition costs explicit, allowing attainable performance and information limits to be studied under the same model. GPU kernel autotuning offers a potential setting for examining how Colombo could adapt its research framework to such a problem. A tuner seeks a fast implementation while limiting costly compilation and measurement. MetaSchedule and recent Helion work illustrate how program structure and learned models can guide this search (Shao et al., 2022; Choi et al., 2026).

To instantiate the specification 𝖲s\mathsf{S}_{s} in Eq. (1), fix a hardware platform, compiler, and measurement protocol. For each instance II, public data uIu_{I} specify the kernel code, tensor specifications, available compiler and hardware information, and permitted prior data. For this initial formulation, assume that these public inputs specify a finite, nonempty set XIX_{I} of configurations whose validity is known before tuning, together with a fixed initial latency predictor mIm_{I}. Discovering configuration validity and accounting for the associated compilation and validation costs would require an extended oracle and resource model. The admissible model class ℐs​(θ)\mathcal{I}_{s}(\theta) restricts the workloads and timing responses under study: the mean latency is fI=mI+rIf_{I}=m_{I}+r_{I}, with unknown residual rI∈ℛs​(uI,θ)r_{I}\in\mathcal{R}_{s}(u_{I};\theta), and timing observations obey declared noise assumptions. The parameters θ\theta quantify the search-space size, residual structure, and noise bounds.

The task 𝖳s\mathsf{T}_{s} is latency minimization. The output space 𝒵s\mathcal{Z}_{s} contains configuration descriptions, with recommendations required to belong to XIX_{I}, and ℓs\ell_{s} measures their latency gap:

𝖳s​[I]\displaystyle\mathsf{T}_{s}[I] :minx∈XIfI(x),ℓs(I,x^)=fI(x^)−minx∈XIfI(x),x^∈XI.\displaystyle:\ \min_{x\in X_{I}}f_{I}(x),\quad\ell_{s}(I,\hat{x})=f_{I}(\hat{x})-\min_{x\in X_{I}}f_{I}(x),\quad\hat{x}\in X_{I}.

The oracle 𝒪s\mathcal{O}_{s} supplies the public inputs and measured latency feedback. The algorithm class 𝒜s\mathcal{A}_{s} consists of tuners that use this information to select configurations, stop, and return a recommendation, under the declared randomization rules. For A∈𝒜sA\in\mathcal{A}_{s}, let AjA_{j} denote its jj-th configuration-selection rule and hj−1h_{j-1} the preceding queries and observations. The interaction is

xj∼Aj(⋅∣uI,hj−1),xj∈XI,Yj=mI(xj)+rI(xj)+ξj.\displaystyle x_{j}\sim A_{j}(\,\cdot\mid u_{I},h_{j-1}),\quad x_{j}\in X_{I},\quad Y_{j}=m_{I}(x_{j})+r_{I}(x_{j})+\xi_{j}.

Here 𝔼[ξj∣uI,hj−1,xj]=0\mathbb{E}[\xi_{j}\mid u_{I},h_{j-1},x_{j}]=0, with noise tails bounded as specified by the Profile. For this formulation, csc_{s} counts calls to the fixed compilation-and-measurement protocol. Thus Ns⋆​(ε,δ,θ)N_{s}^{\star}(\varepsilon,\delta;\theta) is the optimal evaluation complexity for recommending a configuration within ε\varepsilon of the minimum mean latency, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta uniformly over the model class.

The Sensorium would audit these assumptions against hardware evidence, initialize the Complexity Bracket from applicable theoretical guarantees, and identify unresolved regimes. Where a gap remains, the Brain would assign tuning-policy design and lower-bound analyses to Cells under the same information model. The Brain would incorporate each Cell checkpoint into shared memory and update the Live Complexity Bracket. Supported results would return to the Atlas, while systematic prediction failures could lead the Sensorium to formulate new settings. Establishing practical gains would require compiler integration and independent hardware evaluation, including elapsed tuning time with compilation and tuner overhead. The resulting theoretical and empirical evidence would inform subsequent methods and research settings.

4.2  Capability–Challenge Co-Evolution

The algorithm–hardness interaction in oracle optimization suggests a broader form of capability–challenge co-evolution: advances in a method reshape the challenges that remain informative, while those challenges guide further method development. Related learner–environment mechanisms appear in POET, PAIRED, and AutoEnvScaling (Wang et al., 2019; Dennis et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2026). Extending Adversarial Co-Ascent in this direction would use Colombo’s accumulated optimization knowledge to develop training methods and diagnostic challenges.

Methods and predictions.

A concrete scope is the design of optimizers and training procedures for LLM pretraining and fine-tuning. The Setting Profile would specify the available oracle feedback, public model structure, and costs of obtaining and processing information, accommodating both zeroth-order and gradient-based methods (Malladi et al., 2023; Jordan et al., 2024). The research objective would be to improve validation loss at a given training cost and understand transfer across scales (Hoffmann et al., 2022; Qiu et al., 2025). The Algorithm Library could supply candidate update mechanisms and training strategies, while the Hard-Family Library could suggest diagnostic problems and controlled training conditions that test their proposed advantages. Each hypothesis would state its applicability conditions and predictions about improvements in the loss–compute tradeoff and the regimes in which those improvements should persist or disappear.

Co-evolution through evaluation.

Starting from the observed loss–compute frontier, the Sensorium would identify unexplained efficiency differences or failures of transfer. The Brain would organize Cells to investigate candidate methods and diagnostic comparisons across model scales and data regimes. Evaluation would test the predictions at matched training FLOPs, accounting for both model computation and optimizer updates. Complementary evaluations would compare wall-clock time to a pre-specified target on fixed hardware (Kasimbeg et al., 2025). Methods would receive matched tuning allowances; total experimental compute would be tracked separately. As methods improve, subsequent challenges would probe their remaining limitations and guide the next design hypotheses, while fixed reference evaluations preserve comparability.

Frontier renewal and empirical laws.

Reproduced gains would advance the empirical frontier, while systematic prediction failures could motivate revised hypotheses or new oracle settings. The Long-Term Memory would retain the resulting methods, predictions, evidence, and applicability conditions as starting points for subsequent programmes. Across programmes, these records could support the search for empirical laws of AI training: quantitative relations linking algorithmic choices, data, model scale, and computation to learning performance. Candidate relations would be tested for their ability to predict independent experiments in new regimes, providing a basis for quantitative theories of training. Theoretical complexity claims would continue to require proofs under the Setting Profile.

4.3  Toward Autopoietic Science

These directions share a longer-term ambition: advances should renew the questions, methods, and organization through which further research becomes possible. We use Autopoietic Science to name this vision of sustained frontier regeneration, drawing inspiration from autopoiesis (Maturana and Varela, 1980). Colombo takes an initial step in oracle-based optimization, where supported results can reshape the Complexity Atlas, research programmes, and reusable scientific knowledge. Extending this process to experimental optimization would test whether new algorithms, diagnostic challenges, and explanations can jointly sustain further inquiry. The broader aim is a scientific process that continually develops both its understanding and its capacity to investigate what remains unknown.
